title: The First World War and the Rise of Dictatorships
tagline: Causes and course of the Great War, the Treaty of Versailles, and fascism and militarism in Italy, Germany and Japan.

overview.intro: The Great War of 1914 to 1918 destroyed four empires, reshaped Europe, and left a settlement so bitter that within twenty years two of the defeated powers had fallen to dictatorships which set out to destroy it. This chapter treats the causes of the war under the heads examiners call MAIN — militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism — then the course and results, including the Treaty of Versailles and its war-guilt clause, and then the rise of dictatorships in Italy under Mussolini, in Germany under Hitler and in Japan under the military. The link between the two halves of the chapter is the essential point: the dictatorships grew out of the grievances the peace settlement had left unresolved.

facts.label: The spark
facts.value: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip of the Black Hand.

facts.label: The alliances
facts.value: Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy against the Triple Entente of France, Russia and Britain.

facts.label: The peace
facts.value: The Treaty of Versailles of 1919, which imposed the war-guilt clause, reparations, disarmament and territorial losses on Germany.

facts.label: The dictatorships
facts.value: Fascism in Italy from 1922, Nazism in Germany from 1933 and militarism in Japan from the 1930s.

learningOutcomes: Classify the causes of the First World War under militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism, and name the immediate cause.
Describe the course of the war and state its results, including the end of the four empires.
Explain the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles and the German reaction to it.
Account for the rise of fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany, giving the conditions that made them possible.
Describe the rise of militarism in Japan and state how the three dictatorships were alike.

learn.title: The causes of the First World War

blocks.text: The long-term causes are conventionally classified under four heads, and a structured answer names each and gives an instance. Militarism: the great powers were engaged in a naval and army race, with Germany building a fleet to challenge British sea power under the Tirpitz plans and the powers maintaining large standing armies with plans of mobilisation that made diplomacy slow and war fast. Alliances: the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, formed in 1882, faced the Triple Entente of France, Russia and Britain, created by the Franco-Russian alliance of 1894 and the Entente Cordiale of 1904, so that any local quarrel risked dragging in every power. Imperialism: rivalry for colonies and markets, especially in Africa after the conferences of Berlin and Morocco, had already produced the Moroccan and Balkan crises and left the powers suspicious of one another. Nationalism: the assertion of national claims in the Balkans, where Serbia, backed by Russia, sought to unite the South Slavs and threatened the multi-national Austro-Hungarian Empire, and where the Pan-Slav and Pan-German ideas collided. The immediate cause was the assassination at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, by Gavrilo Princip of the Black Hand: Austria declared war on Serbia, Russia mobilised in Serbia’s support, Germany declared war on Russia and France, invaded Belgium under the Schlieffen plan, and Britain declared war on Germany in August 1914.

items: Militarism: the Anglo-German naval race and the mobilisation timetables that turned a crisis into a general war.
Alliances: the Triple Alliance against the Triple Entente, which made a Balkan quarrel a world war.
Imperialism: rivalry over colonies and markets in Africa and Asia, producing the Moroccan and Balkan crises.
Nationalism: Serbian nationalism and Pan-Slavism against Austro-Hungarian and Pan-German ambition in the Balkans.
Immediate cause: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip.
The chain of declarations in July and August 1914 turned a murder into a general European war.

learn.title: The course of the war and its results

blocks.text: The war began with German advances into Belgium and France and a eastern front against Russia, and then settled into trench warfare along the Western Front where millions faced each other for years over a few miles of mud. The war became a war of machines: machine-guns, heavy artillery, poison gas from 1915, the tank from 1916, the submarine and the aeroplane. Turning points came in 1917: the United States entered on the side of the Allies after the sinking of its ships by German submarines and the revelation of the Zimmermann telegram, and Russia left the war after the Bolshevik Revolution and signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. The German offensive of 1918 failed, and the Allies counter-attacked, Germany sued for an armistice on 11 November 1918, and the Kaiser abdicated. The results were enormous: four empires — the German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian — had ended or collapsed; about ten million soldiers died and many more were wounded; new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Finland appeared; and the peace settlement left Germany resentful, Italy dissatisfied and the map of Eastern Europe unstable, while the United States emerged as a creditor and Japan as a power in the Pacific.

items: From mobile advance to trench deadlock on the Western Front, where the war became a war of machines and attrition.
New weapons: machine-guns, heavy artillery, poison gas, the tank, the submarine and the aeroplane.
The war became global, with campaigns in Africa, the Middle East and Asia and the use of colonial troops.
1917 turned the war: the United States entered after the submarine campaign, and Russia left after the Bolshevik Revolution.
The armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the fighting; the Kaiser abdicated and Germany became a republic.
Results: four empires ended, about ten million soldiers died, and new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia appeared.

learn.title: The Treaty of Versailles and the German reaction

blocks.text: The Treaty of Versailles of 28 June 1919 imposed the settlement on Germany, and its terms fall into familiar heads. Territorial: Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France, Eupen and Malmédy to Belgium, North Schleswig to Denmark after a plebiscite, West Prussia and Posen to the new state of Poland, which created the Polish Corridor and left East Prussia separated from Germany, the port of Danzig became a free city, Memel was taken, the Saar basin was placed under the League for fifteen years with its coal given to France, the colonies were taken away as mandates, and the Rhineland was demilitarised. Military: the army was limited to a hundred thousand men, conscription was abolished, the navy was reduced, tanks, a general staff and an air force were forbidden. Financial and moral: Article 231, the war-guilt clause, laid the responsibility for the war on Germany and her allies and justified the demand for reparations, which were fixed in 1921 at a huge sum in gold marks. Germany signed under protest, the German delegation and public called it a dictated peace, and the treaty became the most powerful instrument of Nazi propaganda: the stab-in-the-back legend, the war-guilt lie and the burden of reparations together poisoned the Weimar Republic from its birth.

items: Territorial losses: Alsace-Lorraine to France, West Prussia and Posen to Poland with the Polish Corridor, Danzig as a free city, the colonies as mandates.
The Saar under League administration for fifteen years and the Rhineland demilitarised.
Military limits: an army of a hundred thousand, no conscription, no general staff, no tanks and no air force.
Article 231, the war-guilt clause, and the reparations fixed in 1921.
The German reaction: a dictated peace, the stab-in-the-back legend, and the treaty used as propaganda against the republic.
The treaty’s long effect: it left Germany resentful and provided the grievances on which the Nazi movement fed.

blocks.text: In Italy the dictatorship grew out of disappointment: Italy had joined the Allies in 1915 expecting territory and got little at Versailles, the post-war years brought unemployment, strikes and the fear of a socialist revolution on the Russian model, and the parliamentary government appeared weak. Benito Mussolini, a former socialist journalist who founded the Fascio di Combattimento in 1919 and organised the black-shirted Squadrists against socialists and trade unions, was appointed Prime Minister in October 1922 after the March on Rome, and by 1924 to 1926 he had eliminated opposition parties, murdered the socialist deputy Matteotti, imposed a one-party state, censorship and a secret police, and made himself Il Duce with a corporatist state economy and aggressive foreign policy in Ethiopia from 1935 and Albania from 1939. In Germany the road ran from defeat to dictatorship through the Weimar Republic: the republic was saddled with Versailles, suffered hyperinflation in 1923 which wiped out savings, briefly prospered under the Dawes and Young plans and American loans, and then was destroyed by the world depression after 1929, which threw six million out of work and drove voters to the extremes. Adolf Hitler, appointed Chancellor in January 1933, used the Reichstag fire to suspend civil liberties, passed the Enabling Act which let him legislate without Parliament, banned other parties and trade unions, built the Gestapo and the concentration camps, rearmed in defiance of the treaty, remilitarised the Rhineland in 1936 and drove the German economy to arms production, with propaganda under Goebbels and the Führer principle as the instruments of control.

items: Italy: disappointment at Versailles, unemployment, strikes and the fear of revolution created the conditions for the Fascists.
Mussolini founded the Fascio di Combattimento in 1919, organised the Squadrists and became Prime Minister after the March on Rome of 1922.
By 1926 Italy was a one-party state with censorship, a secret police and the corporate economy under Il Duce.
Germany: Versailles, the hyperinflation of 1923 and the depression after 1929 destroyed faith in the Weimar Republic.
Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933, used the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act to end parliamentary government.
Nazi control rested on the Gestapo, the courts, the propaganda ministry, the banning of parties and unions, and the Führer principle.

Passed after the Reichstag fire, it let the government legislate without Parliament for four years, which is the legal form in which German democracy ended.

items.meaning: The doctrine of Mussolini’s Italy: an authoritarian one-party state, corporatist economy, glorification of the nation and the leader.
National Socialism under Hitler: racial doctrine, extreme nationalism, one-party dictatorship and rearmament.
The principle that the leader’s will is the supreme law, which replaced collective government in Nazi Germany.
The German republic of 1919 to 1933, named after the town where its constitution was drafted.

learn.title: Militarism in Japan and the comparison of the three

blocks.text: Japan’s dictatorship was military rather than party-based, and it grew from imperial ambition frustrated by the world depression. Japan had fought on the Allied side in 1914 to 1918 and gained German concessions in Shandong and the mandates in the Pacific, but the Washington treaties limited its naval strength, and the depression of 1929 destroyed the export markets on which its economy depended. The army, which had its own political base and answered to the Emperor rather than to the Diet, Manchuria in 1931, establishing the puppet state of Manchukuo, and killed the prime ministers who opposed expansion; the Marco Polo Bridge incident of July 1937 opened the war in China, and the military increasingly controlled the government until the surrender of 1945. The three dictatorships can be compared on common ground: each grew out of a national humiliation or economic disaster; each replaced parliamentary government with a one-party state led by a single ruler; each used propaganda, censorship and a secret police; each glorified militarism and national or racial destiny; and each needed constant success abroad to justify itself at home, which is why all three turned to aggression in the 1930s and made a second world war inevitable.

items: Japan’s disappointment with the post-war settlements, especially the naval limitation, fed military nationalism.
The world depression destroyed Japan’s export economy and strengthened the army’s argument for expansion.
The army seized Manchuria in 1931 and set up Manchukuo, defying the League of Nations.
The Marco Polo Bridge incident of 1937 began the full-scale war in China.
Common features: humiliation or crisis, one-party rule, propaganda and police control, militarism and expansion.
The connection to the war: each dictatorship required external success to survive, which made aggression and a second world war inevitable.

questions.explanation: It faced the Triple Entente of France, Russia and Britain.

questions.explanation: Conscription was abolished and tanks, a general staff and an air force were forbidden.

questions.prompt: Explain the terms of the Treaty of Versailles under the territorial and military heads.
questions.answer: Territorially, Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France, Eupen and Malmédy to Belgium, West Prussia and Posen to Poland with the Polish Corridor separating East Prussia from the rest of Germany, Danzig was made a free city, Memel was taken, the colonies were confiscated as mandates of the League of Nations, the Saar was placed under the League for fifteen years and the Rhineland was demilitarised. Militarily, the army was limited to a hundred thousand men, conscription was abolished, the navy was greatly reduced, and tanks, a general staff and an air force were forbidden, while an occupation of the Rhineland guaranteed the terms.
questions.explanation: Both heads must be given in full: the territorial losses and the military restrictions.

questions.prompt: State the results of the First World War.
questions.answer: Four empires ended — the German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian — and new states such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Finland appeared. About ten million soldiers died and many more were wounded, and the war was fought on four continents with the use of colonial troops. Economically the United States emerged as a creditor and Japan as a power in the Pacific, while Europe was left with huge debts and ruined regions. Politically the settlement left Germany resentful, Italy dissatisfied and the map of Eastern Europe unstable, which prepared the ground for a second war.
questions.explanation: Empires, casualties, new states and the unstable settlement are the four strands.

questions.prompt: Mention two causes of the rise of dictatorship in Germany.
questions.answer: The humiliation of the Treaty of Versailles, with its war-guilt clause and reparations, embittered Germans against the republic that signed it. The economic collapse after 1929 threw millions out of work and destroyed faith in parliamentary government, and the hyperinflation of 1923 had already ruined the savings of the middle class. Weak coalition governments ruling by emergency decree under Article 48 completed the discredit of the Weimar Republic.
questions.explanation: Any two of Versailles, hyperinflation, the depression, weak coalitions and the stab-in-the-back legend.

questions.prompt: Explain the main causes of the First World War and show how the assassination at Sarajevo led to a general war.
questions.answer: The long-term causes are usually classified as militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism. Militarism meant the arms races, above all the Anglo-German naval race, and the mobilisation timetables that made it impossible to wait while diplomacy worked. The alliance system divided Europe into the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy and the Triple Entente of France, Russia and Britain, so that any quarrel risked a general war. Imperialist rivalry over colonies, especially in Africa, produced the Moroccan and Balkan crises and a lasting suspicion between the powers. Nationalism in the Balkans, where Serbia backed by Russia sought to unite the South Slavs and threatened the Austro-Hungarian Empire, supplied the inflammable material. The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip of the Black Hand. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, Russia mobilised in Serbia’s defence, Germany declared war on Russia and France and invaded Belgium under the Schlieffen plan, and Britain declared war on Germany in August 1914 in defence of Belgian neutrality — so a murder in the Balkans became a general European war within a month.
questions.explanation: The four heads with instances, then the assassination and the exact chain of declarations that followed it.

questions.prompt: How far did the Treaty of Versailles prepare the ground for the rise of Nazism in Germany?
questions.answer: The treaty prepared the ground in three ways. Politically, Article 231 assigned the guilt of the war to Germany alone, which was resented even by those who accepted defeat, and the phrase dictated peace suggested that the republic had submitted rather than negotiated — the leaders of the Weimar Republic were therefore attacked as the criminals of November who had stabbed the army in the back. Economically, reparations fixed in 1921 burdened the budget, and when Germany fell behind in payments France occupied the Ruhr in 1923, which brought the hyperinflation that wiped out the savings of the middle class; even after the Dawes and Young plans eased the burden, the loans that funded recovery were American and collapsed after 1929, so the depression fell on a country already wounded. Territorially, the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, the Polish Corridor and the colonies, and the demilitarisation of the Rhineland, gave the Nazis specific grievances they could name in every speech, and Hitler’s rearmament and remilitarisation were presented as the restoration of a nation’s honour. Against this it must be said that the treaty alone did not create Nazism: the depression, the weakness of the coalition parties, the use of Article 48 and Hitler’s own organisation were equally necessary, and many signatories of the treaty elsewhere in Europe did not become dictatorships. The balanced answer is that the treaty supplied the grievance and the propaganda, and the depression supplied the mass audience.
questions.explanation: Three channels — political legitimacy, economic burden and territorial grievance — plus the counter-argument, closing with the joint effect of treaty and depression.

questions.prompt: Compare the rise of dictatorships in Italy, Germany and Japan.
questions.answer: Each dictatorship grew from a national crisis: in Italy, disappointment at the peace settlement and the fear of a socialist revolution; in Germany, Versailles, hyperinflation and the depression; in Japan, the limitations imposed by the naval treaties and the collapse of export markets after 1929. The routes to power differed: Mussolini was appointed Prime Minister after the March on Rome of 1922 and then dismantled parliament; Hitler was appointed Chancellor in January 1933 and used the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act to legislate without parliament; in Japan the army, which answered to the Emperor rather than to the Diet, killed opposing ministers and took control of policy after the seizure of Manchuria in 1931. The forms of control were alike in essentials — a one-party state, a single leader or a military clique, propaganda, censorship and a secret police, and the suppression of trade unions and opposition parties. Their ambitions were alike too: Italy attacked Ethiopia, Germany rearmed and absorbed Austria and Czechoslovakia, and Japan invaded Manchuria and China, and in each case external aggression was needed to justify the regime at home. The shared pattern is therefore crisis, one-party control and expansion, with differences only in the route and the style of leadership.
questions.explanation: Shared conditions, differing routes, common instruments of control and common expansion, each illustrated with one instance.
